statement: The plain base's terse register is intrinsically weaker than the deliberative '\nOkay' register by about 15-20 points at any temperature, and its extra loss at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 is mostly a stopping-and-grading failure, not reasoning derailed by tail tokens and then rescued by self-checks: the terse register often reaches an answer and then fails to end cleanly, running on into further answers or invented problems that the last-marker grader v3 scores, while the deliberative register ends on one final answer; 'Wait'/'Hmm' self-checks mark long, hard problems and protect nothing.
why_strongest: It accounts for every number in tests.json without a noise-robustness step. (1) Non-self-opened answers drop 0.158 from T 0.6 to T 1.0 on the same problems. Hotter sampling makes the terse register miss end-of-text, and v3 then reads the run-on. Only rows that run on are lost, so the drop is smaller than the theory's 0.29. (2) At T 0.6, non-self-opened answers are 0.155 below the cue, even though the cue loops on 119 problems at T 0.6. Self-opened answers beat non-self-opened ones by 0.206. These are register gaps at cool temperature, where the theory predicted -0.10 and +0.09. (3) Within non-self-opened T 1.0 answers, rows with 'Wait'/'Hmm' beat rows without by 0.356, and they sit only 0.075 (MATH-500) or 0.10 (hard328) below the cue. Marker rows are deliberative-register derivations that finish on one answer. Unmarked rows are mostly short commit-and-continue texts, where the terse register's stopping failure lives. The marker selects the register; it does not rescue anything. (4) Facts fit: cued T1 rows show 0 first-marker recoveries and 0 first-right discordances, because the deliberative register does not run on, and self-opened plain answers match cued accuracy (0.0). (5) before.jsonl fits: the only v3 right-to-wrong flip was a plain T 1.0 answer that invented and answered a new problem after its real answer. v1/v2 found no answer in 166 of 500 plain T 1.0 texts. The plain base loses about 28 points at T 1.0 on short problems, where answers end early and can run on, but holds on the longest quartile. Base answers of <= 2,000 tokens are 95 % right in the cued register. Grader effects are large here (v1 to v3 moved 113 items).

tests.experiment: Within the cued base's MATH-500 answers at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0: accuracy of answers containing 'Wait' or 'Hmm' minus accuracy of answers containing neither.
tests.recipe: File: S3 r4/base_rl-02/out/T1.jsonl (s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r4/base_rl-02/out/T1.jsonl; base, cue, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, MATH-500). If more than one row exists for a problem_index, keep the first in file order. Score each kept row with grader v3 (studies/rlneurons/grader/rln4_grader_v3.py) from its text and gold. Cap-hit rows are kept and keep whatever score v3 gives; an empty extraction counts 0. Group M = kept rows whose full text field contains the case-sensitive substring 'Wait' or the case-sensitive substring 'Hmm' (or both); group N = all other kept rows. Statistic: (mean v3 score of M) - (mean v3 score of N). If either group is empty, report nothing.
tests.theory_should_say: The theory makes self-checking the reason the deliberative register survives untruncated sampling, so cued answers that check themselves should be at least as accurate as those that do not (about +0.05). In the rival, checks only mark long, hard problems, and unchecked cued answers are short and nearly always right, so the difference is clearly negative.

tests.experiment: The same contrast on the harder clean 328: within cued base answers at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, accuracy of answers containing 'Wait' or 'Hmm' minus accuracy of answers containing neither.
tests.recipe: File: S3 r5/day1_hard328-01/abaybektursun-1114-151534-e72c/answers.jsonl (s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r5/day1_hard328-01/abaybektursun-1114-151534-e72c/answers.jsonl; base, cue, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0, hard328). If more than one row exists for a problem_index, keep the row with the smallest attempt value (with no attempt field, the first in file order). Score = the score_v3 column; a null or missing score_v3 counts 0. Cap-hit rows are kept with their score_v3. Group M = kept rows whose full text field contains the case-sensitive substring 'Wait' or the case-sensitive substring 'Hmm' (or both); group N = all other kept rows. Statistic: (mean score of M) - (mean score of N). If either group is empty, report nothing.
tests.theory_should_say: Under the theory, self-checks are what lets the deliberative register survive full-temperature noise, so checked cued answers should be no worse than unchecked ones (about 0, maybe slightly positive). The rival expects a strongly negative gap: unchecked answers are the few short, easy ones, and the checked ones include all 77 cap hits.

tests.experiment: Gold-in-text excess at T 1.0 over T 0.6 for the plain base's finished, wrong, non-self-opened answers on problems with an integer gold of absolute value >= 10: the share whose text contains the gold number, T 1.0 minus T 0.6.
tests.recipe: Files: S3 T3.jsonl (s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r4/modal_t3-01/t3/T3.jsonl; base, plain, T 1.0 / top-p 1.0) and S3 r3/base-01/out/P_math500.jsonl (s3://pg-lineage-769063704696/results/rlneurons/r3/base-01/out/P_math500.jsonl; base, plain, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95). In T3 keep the first row per problem_index in file order; in P_math500 keep, per problem_index, the row with the smallest sample value. Score each kept row with grader v3 (studies/rlneurons/grader/rln4_grader_v3.py) from text and gold, where an empty extraction counts 0. Self-opened = the first 60 characters of text contain the substring '\nOkay' (a newline immediately followed by 'Okay'). In each file separately, keep rows that are not self-opened, have cap_hit false and v3 score 0, and whose gold, after removing all '$' and whitespace and, if it is wholly wrapped in \boxed{...}, taking the inside, fully matches ^-?\d+$ with absolute value >= 10. For each kept row, let t = text with every comma between digits deleted (regex (?<=\d),(?=\d) replaced by ''). Let g = the digits of the gold's absolute value, written without leading zeros. The row is a hit if the regex (?<![0-9])g(?![0-9]) matches anywhere in t. F(file) = hits / kept rows. Statistic: F(T3) - F(P_math500). If either file has no kept rows, report nothing.
tests.theory_should_say: In the theory, wrong terse answers at T 1.0 are reasoning derailed by tail tokens, so they reach the gold no more often than the genuine mistakes at T 0.6 (about 0.0). In the rival, many T 1.0 failures wrote the right number and then lost it by running on, so the share is clearly higher at T 1.0.
